**Algebra of series and tails.** If \(\sum a_n = A\) and \(\sum b_n = B\), then \(\sum (a_n \pm b_n) = A \pm B\) and \(\sum c\,a_n = cA\) for every constant \(c\); these follow from the limit laws applied to partial sums. Deleting or changing finitely many terms does not affect convergence, because it changes every later partial sum by the same constant. Thus \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\) and \(\sum_{n=N}^{\infty} a_n\) converge or diverge together; when they converge, their sums differ by \(a_1 + \cdots + a_{N-1}\). This is why each test in the following sections needs its hypotheses only for all \(n\) beyond some index. Finally, if \(\sum a_n\) converges and \(\sum b_n\) diverges, then \(\sum(a_n + b_n)\) diverges, since otherwise \(\sum b_n = \sum(a_n + b_n) - \sum a_n\) would converge.

**Common mistake.** Concluding that a series converges because its terms tend to 0. The divergence test can prove divergence and nothing else; when \(a_n \to 0\) it is silent, and another test must be used. The harmonic series is the standing counterexample.

options: The series converges, since its terms become negligible.
Nothing: the series may converge or diverge, and another test is needed.
The series diverges, by the divergence test.
The series converges and its sum is 0.
questions.prompt: You have shown that \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0\). What may you conclude about \(\sum a_n\) from this fact alone?
questions.why: The theorem says convergence implies \(a_n \to 0\); the converse is false. The harmonic series has \(\frac1n \to 0\) and diverges, while \(\sum \frac1{n^2}\) has terms tending to 0 and converges. The divergence test applies only when the limit of the terms is nonzero or does not exist, and the sum of a series is the limit of its partial sums, not of its terms.

questions.model: Write \(s_{2^k} = 1 + \frac12 + \sum_{j=2}^{k} B_j\), where \(B_j = \frac{1}{2^{j-1}+1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{2^j}\). The block \(B_j\) has \(2^j - 2^{j-1} = 2^{j-1}\) terms, and each is at least the last one, \(\frac{1}{2^j}\). Hence \(B_j \ge 2^{j-1}\cdot\frac1{2^j} = \frac12\), and \(s_{2^k} \ge 1 + \frac12 + (k-1)\cdot\frac12 = 1 + \frac k2\). The partial sums are nondecreasing (the terms are positive) and the subsequence \(s_{2^k}\) is unbounded, so \(s_n \to \infty\) and the series diverges. This is consistent with \(\frac1n \to 0\): the theorem says that convergence forces the terms to tend to 0, not that terms tending to 0 force convergence. Here the terms shrink too slowly; each doubling of the number of terms adds at least \(\frac12\).
questions.prompt: Prove that the harmonic series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac1n\) diverges by showing that \(s_{2^k} \ge 1 + \frac k2\) for every \(k \ge 1\). Then explain why this does not contradict the fact that \(\frac1n \to 0\).
rubric: Groups the terms of \(s_{2^k}\) into \(1\), \(\frac12\), and blocks from \(\frac{1}{2^{j-1}+1}\) to \(\frac1{2^j}\) for \(j = 2, \dots, k\).
Shows each block has \(2^{j-1}\) terms each at least \(\frac1{2^j}\), so each block is at least \(\frac12\).
Concludes \(s_{2^k} \ge 1 + \frac k2\), so the nondecreasing partial sums are unbounded and the series diverges.
Explains that terms tending to 0 is necessary but not sufficient for convergence, so there is no contradiction.
questions.why: This argument (due to Oresme, fourteenth century) is the standard example showing that the divergence test is one-directional.

questions.model: Let \(f(x) = x\sin\frac1x = \frac{\sin(1/x)}{1/x}\). With \(u = \frac1x\), as \(x \to \infty\), \(u \to 0^+\) and \(\frac{\sin u}{u} \to 1\). So \(a_n = n\sin\frac1n \to 1 \ne 0\), and by the divergence test the series diverges.
questions.prompt: Determine whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n\sin\frac1n\) converges. Name the test you use and compute the limit that it requires.
rubric: Computes \(\lim_{n\to\infty} n\sin\frac1n = 1\), e.g. via \(u = \frac1x \to 0^+\) and \(\frac{\sin u}{u} \to 1\).
Observes that the limit is not 0.
Concludes by the divergence test that the series diverges.
questions.why: Always check the limit of the terms first. Here it is 1, so no further work is needed.

sections.title: The divergence test and the harmonic series

sections.md:
The harmonic series showed that deciding convergence can require more than looking at the terms. For series with nonnegative terms there is a clean criterion: the partial sums are nondecreasing, so by the monotone convergence theorem the series converges if and only if its partial sums are bounded above. The integral test finds such a bound, or rules one out, by comparing partial sums with areas under a curve, which reduces the question to an improper integral.

> **Integral test.** Let \(f\) be continuous, positive and decreasing on \([1, \infty)\), and let \(a_n = f(n)\). Then \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\) and \(\int_1^{\infty} f(x)\,dx\) either both converge or both diverge. By the remark on tails, it suffices that the hypotheses hold on some interval \([N, \infty)\), with the integral taken from \(N\).

**Why it is true.** Because \(f\) is decreasing, its smallest value on \([k-1, k]\) is \(f(k) = a_k\), so the rectangle of height \(a_k\) over that interval lies under the curve: \(a_k \le \int_{k-1}^{k} f(x)\,dx\). Adding these inequalities for \(k = 2, \dots, n\),
\[ s_n - a_1 \le \int_1^{n} f(x)\,dx. \]
Similarly, the largest value of \(f\) on \([k, k+1]\) is \(a_k\), so \(\int_k^{k+1} f(x)\,dx \le a_k\); adding for \(k = 1, \dots, n\) gives \(\int_1^{n+1} f(x)\,dx \le s_n\). If the integral converges, the first inequality bounds \(s_n\) by \(a_1 + \int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx\), and the nondecreasing sequence \(\{s_n\}\) converges. If the integral diverges, it diverges to \(\infty\) because \(f > 0\), and the second inequality forces \(s_n \to \infty\). For the harmonic series the second inequality reads \(s_n \ge \ln(n+1)\).

In the graph, the shaded rectangles have heights \(a_2, \dots, a_{10}\) for \(a_n = \frac{1}{n^p}\) and lie beneath \(y = \frac{1}{x^p}\). Drag \(p\) and watch the tail of the curve: the shaded area never exceeds the area under the curve, and that area stays bounded as the right endpoint moves out exactly when \(p > 1\).

```plot
x: 0, 10
y: 0, 1.1
slider: p, 0.5, 3, 2 | p
f: 1/x^p | y = 1/x^p
shade: 1/ceil(x)^p, 1.001, 10 | rectangles of heights a₂, …, a₁₀
```

**The \(p\)-series.** For a real constant \(p\), the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^p}\) is called a **\(p\)-series**.

> **Theorem.** The \(p\)-series converges if \(p > 1\) and diverges if \(p \le 1\).

If \(p \le 0\), the terms do not tend to 0 (they equal 1 or grow), so the divergence test applies. If \(p > 0\), then \(f(x) = x^{-p}\) is continuous, positive and decreasing on \([1, \infty)\), and the chapter on improper integrals showed that \(\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx\) converges exactly when \(p > 1\). So \(\sum \frac{1}{n^2}\) and \(\sum \frac{1}{n^{1.01}}\) converge, while \(\sum \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\) diverges.

**Worked example.** Decide whether \(\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(\ln n)^2}\) converges. Let \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x(\ln x)^2}\) on \([2, \infty)\). It is continuous and positive there, and decreasing because its denominator is a product of positive increasing functions. With \(u = \ln x\),
\[ \int_2^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x(\ln x)^2} = \int_{\ln 2}^{\infty} \frac{du}{u^2} = \frac{1}{\ln 2}, \]
so the series converges. The same substitution shows that \(\sum_{n=2}^\infty \frac{1}{n \ln n}\) diverges, since \(\int_2^b \frac{dx}{x\ln x} = \ln(\ln b) - \ln(\ln 2) \to \infty\).

**Estimating the sum.** The same rectangles bound the **remainder** \(R_n = S - s_n = \sum_{k=n+1}^{\infty} a_k\), the error made by stopping after \(n\) terms. Under the hypotheses of the integral test,
\[ \int_{n+1}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx \le R_n \le \int_{n}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx. \]
For \(\sum \frac{1}{n^3}\) with \(n = 10\): \(s_{10} \approx 1.197532\), \(\int_{10}^\infty x^{-3}\,dx = \frac{1}{200} = 0.005\) and \(\int_{11}^\infty x^{-3}\,dx = \frac{1}{242} \approx 0.004132\). Therefore \(1.201664 \le S \le 1.202532\); the true value is \(1.2020569\ldots\).

**Common mistakes.** First, reading the value of the integral as the value of the series. The integral decides convergence only: \(\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^2} = 1\), but \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} \approx 1.645\). Second, skipping the hypotheses. The rectangle inequalities used that \(f\) is decreasing, and without it the test can fail: \(f(x) = \sin^2(\pi x) + \frac{1}{x^2}\) is positive and continuous, \(\sum f(n) = \sum \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges, yet \(\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx\) diverges. Verify positivity, continuity and (eventual) decrease, usually through the sign of \(f'\).

questions.model: Let \(f(x) = xe^{-x^2}\). It is continuous and positive on \([1, \infty)\), and \(f'(x) = e^{-x^2} - 2x^2e^{-x^2} = e^{-x^2}(1 - 2x^2) < 0\) for \(x \ge 1\), so \(f\) is decreasing there. With \(u = x^2\), \(du = 2x\,dx\): \(\int_1^b xe^{-x^2}\,dx = \frac12\left(e^{-1} - e^{-b^2}\right) \to \frac{1}{2e}\) as \(b \to \infty\). The integral converges, so by the integral test the series converges. (Its sum is not \(\frac1{2e}\); the test only decides convergence.)
questions.prompt: Use the integral test to decide whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n e^{-n^2}\) converges. Verify each hypothesis of the test explicitly.
rubric: Takes \(f(x) = xe^{-x^2}\) and notes it is continuous and positive on \([1, \infty)\).
Shows \(f\) is decreasing: \(f'(x) = e^{-x^2}(1 - 2x^2) < 0\) for \(x \ge 1\).
Evaluates \(\int_1^\infty xe^{-x^2}\,dx = \frac{1}{2e}\) with the substitution \(u = x^2\) and a limit.
Concludes that the series converges, without claiming its sum equals \(\frac{1}{2e}\).
questions.why: The integral test has three hypotheses, and decrease is the one that needs work; the sign of \(f'\) settles it.

questions.prompt: For \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^3}\), the integral bound gives \(R_n \le \int_n^{\infty} x^{-3}\,dx\). Find the smallest \(n\) for which this bound guarantees \(R_n < 0.0005\).

questions.model: Let \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x(\ln x)^p}\) on \([2, \infty)\). For \(p > 0\), \(x\) and \((\ln x)^p\) are positive, continuous and increasing there, so \(f\) is continuous, positive and decreasing. With \(u = \ln x\), \(du = \frac{dx}{x}\), \(\int_2^\infty \frac{dx}{x(\ln x)^p} = \int_{\ln 2}^\infty u^{-p}\,du\), which converges if and only if \(p > 1\). By the integral test, the series converges for \(p > 1\) and diverges for \(0 < p \le 1\).
questions.prompt: For which \(p > 0\) does \(\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n(\ln n)^p}\) converge? Justify your answer with the integral test, including its hypotheses.
rubric: Takes \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x(\ln x)^p}\) and verifies it is continuous, positive and decreasing on \([2, \infty)\) for \(p > 0\).
Substitutes \(u = \ln x\) to reduce the integral to \(\int_{\ln 2}^\infty u^{-p}\,du\).
Uses the \(p\)-integral result: converges exactly when \(p > 1\).
Concludes the series converges for \(p > 1\) and diverges for \(0 < p \le 1\).
questions.why: The logarithm slows the terms only slightly: the dividing line is still \(p = 1\), as for \(p\)-series. At \(p = 1\) the integral is \(\ln(\ln b) - \ln(\ln 2)\), which diverges extremely slowly.

sections.title: The integral test, p-series, and remainder estimates

sections.md:
The integral test needs a function that can be integrated. Most series, such as \(\sum \frac{1}{n^2 + 1}\) or \(\sum \frac{1}{2^n - 1}\), are instead close to a geometric series or a \(p\)-series whose behaviour is already known, and the comparison tests turn that closeness into a proof. Throughout this section the terms must be nonnegative.

> **Direct comparison test.** Suppose \(0 \le a_n \le b_n\) for all \(n \ge N\).
> 1. If \(\sum b_n\) converges, then \(\sum a_n\) converges.
> 2. If \(\sum a_n\) diverges, then \(\sum b_n\) diverges.

*Proof of 1.* Discarding the first \(N - 1\) terms of each series does not affect convergence. The partial sums of \(\sum_{n \ge N} a_n\) are nondecreasing, because the terms are nonnegative, and bounded above by the finite number \(\sum_{n\ge N} b_n\). By the monotone convergence theorem they converge. Part 2 is the contrapositive of part 1.

The logic runs one way: smaller than a convergent series gives convergence, and larger than a divergent series gives divergence. Being smaller than a divergent series, or larger than a convergent one, gives no information.

**Worked example 1.** \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2 + 1}\): since \(0 < \frac{1}{n^2+1} < \frac{1}{n^2}\) and \(\sum \frac{1}{n^2}\) is a convergent \(p\)-series, the series converges.

**Worked example 2.** \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\ln n}{n}\): for \(n \ge 3\), \(\ln n > 1\), so \(\frac{\ln n}{n} > \frac1n > 0\). The harmonic series diverges, hence so does this series.

**When the inequality points the wrong way.** For \(\sum \frac{1}{2^n - 1}\) the natural comparison is \(\sum \frac{1}{2^n}\), which converges; but \(\frac{1}{2^n - 1} > \frac{1}{2^n}\), so direct comparison says nothing. What matters is that the two terms are nearly proportional for large \(n\).

> **Limit comparison test.** Suppose \(a_n > 0\) and \(b_n > 0\) for all \(n \ge N\), and \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = c\) with \(0 < c < \infty\). Then \(\sum a_n\) and \(\sum b_n\) either both converge or both diverge.

*Why.* Since the ratio tends to \(c > 0\), for all large \(n\) it lies between \(\frac c2\) and \(\frac{3c}{2}\), so \(\frac c2\, b_n < a_n < \frac{3c}{2}\, b_n\). If \(\sum b_n\) converges, the right inequality and direct comparison make \(\sum a_n\) converge; if \(\sum b_n\) diverges, the left inequality makes \(\sum a_n\) diverge. If \(c = 0\), only the right inequality survives: when \(\sum b_n\) converges, so does \(\sum a_n\). If \(c = \infty\), only the left survives: when \(\sum b_n\) diverges, so does \(\sum a_n\).

For \(\sum \frac{1}{2^n - 1}\), \(\frac{1/(2^n - 1)}{1/2^n} = \frac{2^n}{2^n - 1} \to 1\), so the series converges.

**Choosing \(b_n\).** Keep only the dominant part of the numerator and of the denominator. **Worked example 3.** For \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2n + 3}{\sqrt{n^5 + 1}}\), the dominant parts give \(\frac{2n}{n^{5/2}} = \frac{2}{n^{3/2}}\), so take \(b_n = \frac{1}{n^{3/2}}\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(n^{5/2}\),
\[ \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \frac{(2n + 3)\,n^{3/2}}{\sqrt{n^5 + 1}} = \frac{2 + 3/n}{\sqrt{1 + 1/n^5}} \to 2, \]
which is positive and finite. Since \(\sum \frac{1}{n^{3/2}}\) is a \(p\)-series with \(p = \frac32 > 1\), the given series converges.

**Common mistakes.** Comparing in the wrong direction, as above. Applying either test to series with negative terms: \(-1 \le \frac{1}{n^2}\) for every \(n\), yet \(\sum(-1)\) diverges, so the hypothesis \(0 \le a_n\) is essential. And, in the limit comparison test, drawing a conclusion when the limit is 0 or \(\infty\) without checking which of the two surviving cases applies.

questions.model: For \(n \ge 1\), \(3n^2 - 1 > 0\) and \(n^3 + 2n + 5 > 0\), so the terms are positive. The dominant parts are \(3n^2\) and \(n^3\), suggesting \(b_n = \frac1n\). Then \(\frac{a_n}{b_n} = \frac{3n^3 - n}{n^3 + 2n + 5} = \frac{3 - 1/n^2}{1 + 2/n^2 + 5/n^3} \to 3\), with \(0 < 3 < \infty\). Since \(\sum \frac1n\) diverges, the series diverges by the limit comparison test.
questions.prompt: Determine whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{3n^2 - 1}{n^3 + 2n + 5}\) converges. State the comparison series you choose, why you chose it, and compute the limit the test requires.
rubric: Notes the terms are positive for \(n \ge 1\).
Chooses \(b_n = \frac1n\) from the dominant parts \(\frac{3n^2}{n^3}\).
Computes \(\lim \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \lim \frac{3n^3 - n}{n^3 + 2n + 5} = 3\), which is positive and finite.
Concludes divergence by the limit comparison test with the divergent harmonic series.
questions.why: The terms behave like \(\frac3n\) for large \(n\). Direct comparison with \(\frac1n\) would need an inequality that is awkward to establish; the limit comparison test avoids it.

questions.model: Direct comparison with a convergent series requires \(a_n \le b_n\). The student has \(a_n > b_n\), and a series whose terms exceed those of a convergent series may converge or diverge, so nothing follows. A correct proof: for \(n \ge 2\), \(n^2 \ge 2\), so \(n^2 - 1 \ge n^2 - \frac{n^2}{2} = \frac{n^2}{2}\), hence \(0 < \frac1{n^2 - 1} \le \frac{2}{n^2}\). Since \(\sum \frac{2}{n^2}\) converges (a multiple of a \(p\)-series with \(p = 2\)), the series converges by direct comparison. Alternatively, \(\frac{1/(n^2-1)}{1/n^2} = \frac{n^2}{n^2 - 1} \to 1\), and the limit comparison test applies.
questions.prompt: A student wants to show that \(\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2 - 1}\) converges and writes: \"\(\frac{1}{n^2 - 1} > \frac{1}{n^2}\), and \(\sum \frac1{n^2}\) converges, so the series converges by the comparison test.\" Explain what is wrong, then give a correct proof.
rubric: Identifies that the inequality points the wrong way: being larger than the terms of a convergent series gives no information.
Gives a valid proof: e.g. \(n^2 - 1 \ge \frac{n^2}{2}\) for \(n \ge 2\), so \(0 < \frac1{n^2-1} \le \frac2{n^2}\), and direct comparison; or limit comparison with \(\frac1{n^2}\) (limit 1).
Cites the convergence of the \(p\)-series with \(p = 2\) and concludes convergence.
questions.why: In fact the series telescopes: \(\frac{1}{n^2 - 1} = \frac12\left(\frac1{n-1} - \frac1{n+1}\right)\), and its sum is \(\frac12\left(1 + \frac12\right) = \frac34\).

sections.title: The direct and limit comparison tests

sections.md:
Every test so far requires nonnegative terms, and for such series convergence simply means bounded partial sums. When the terms change sign, cancellation between them can make a series converge even though the series of their sizes diverges. This section treats the most common case, in which the signs strictly alternate.

> **Definition.** An **alternating series** is a series of the form \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n+1} b_n = b_1 - b_2 + b_3 - \cdots\) or \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n b_n\), where \(b_n > 0\) for all \(n\).

> **Alternating series test (Leibniz).** If \(b_n > 0\), \(b_{n+1} \le b_n\) for all \(n\), and \(\lim_{n\to\infty} b_n = 0\), then \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n+1} b_n\) converges. It suffices that the inequality \(b_{n+1} \le b_n\) hold from some index on.

**Why it is true.** Consider the even-indexed partial sums. Grouping in pairs,
\[ s_{2m} = (b_1 - b_2) + (b_3 - b_4) + \cdots + (b_{2m-1} - b_{2m}), \]
and each bracket is nonnegative because the \(b_n\) do not increase, so \(\{s_{2m}\}\) is nondecreasing. Grouping differently,
\[ s_{2m} = b_1 - (b_2 - b_3) - \cdots - (b_{2m-2} - b_{2m-1}) - b_{2m} \le b_1, \]
so \(\{s_{2m}\}\) is bounded above. By the monotone convergence theorem, \(s_{2m} \to S\) for some \(S\). The odd partial sums satisfy \(s_{2m+1} = s_{2m} + b_{2m+1} \to S + 0 = S\). The even and odd subsequences have the same limit, so \(s_n \to S\), as shown in the previous chapter. Both hypotheses were used: monotonicity to control the brackets, and \(b_n \to 0\) to make the odd and even partial sums meet.

**The alternating harmonic series.** The series \(1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \frac14 + \cdots\) satisfies the hypotheses with \(b_n = \frac1n\), so it converges, although the harmonic series itself diverges. Its sum is \(\ln 2\), a fact proved with Taylor series later in the course. The graph shows its partial sums: they land alternately above and below \(\ln 2\), each step shorter than the one before.

```plot
x: 0, 15
y: 0.4, 1.05
hline: log(2) | ln 2
point: 1, 1.0000
point: 2, 0.5000
point: 3, 0.8333
point: 4, 0.5833
point: 5, 0.7833
point: 6, 0.6167
point: 7, 0.7595
point: 8, 0.6345
point: 9, 0.7456
point: 10, 0.6456
point: 11, 0.7365
point: 12, 0.6532
point: 13, 0.7301
point: 14, 0.6587
```

**Error estimate.** The picture suggests that the sum always lies between two consecutive partial sums. That is true, and it yields an error bound.

> **Alternating series estimation theorem.** Under the hypotheses of the alternating series test, the remainder \(R_n = S - s_n\) satisfies \(|R_n| \le b_{n+1}\): the error made by stopping after \(n\) terms is at most the size of the first omitted term. Moreover, \(R_n\) has the same sign as that first omitted term.

**Worked example.** Estimate \(S = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^4}\) with five terms. Here \(b_n = \frac{1}{n^4}\) is positive, decreasing and tends to 0. Then \(s_5 = 1 - \frac1{16} + \frac1{81} - \frac1{256} + \frac1{625} \approx 0.947539\), and \(|S - s_5| \le b_6 = \frac{1}{1296} \approx 0.000772\). The first omitted term, \(-\frac{1}{1296}\), is negative, so \(s_5\) overestimates, and \(0.946768 \le S \le 0.947539\). The exact value is \(\frac{7\pi^4}{720} \approx 0.947033\).

**Common mistakes.** First, omitting the monotonicity check. The series \(1 - \frac14 + \frac13 - \frac1{16} + \frac15 - \frac1{36} + \cdots\), whose odd-position terms are \(\frac1n\) and even-position terms \(\frac1{n^2}\), alternates and has terms tending to 0, but its terms do not decrease, and it diverges: \(s_{2m} = \sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{1}{2k-1} - \sum_{k=1}^m \frac{1}{4k^2}\), where the first sum tends to \(\infty\) and the second stays bounded. Second, concluding divergence because the test does not apply. The test gives a sufficient condition only. If \(b_n \not\to 0\), use the divergence test; if \(\{b_n\}\) is not eventually monotone, another argument is needed.

questions.model: The series is alternating with \(b_n = \frac{\sqrt n}{n+1} > 0\). Dividing numerator and denominator by \(n\), \(b_n = \frac{1/\sqrt n}{1 + 1/n} \to \frac{0}{1} = 0\). For monotonicity let \(f(x) = \frac{\sqrt x}{x + 1}\). By the quotient rule, \(f'(x) = \frac{\frac{1}{2\sqrt x}(x+1) - \sqrt x}{(x+1)^2} = \frac{1 - x}{2\sqrt x\,(x+1)^2}\), which is \(\le 0\) for \(x \ge 1\). So \(b_{n+1} \le b_n\) for all \(n \ge 1\). By the alternating series test the series converges.
questions.prompt: Show that \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{n+1}\frac{\sqrt n}{n+1}\) converges. Verify each hypothesis of the test you use; the decrease of the terms requires an argument.
rubric: Identifies the series as alternating with \(b_n = \frac{\sqrt n}{n+1} > 0\).
Shows \(b_n \to 0\), e.g. \(b_n = \frac{1/\sqrt n}{1 + 1/n}\).
Shows \(\{b_n\}\) is nonincreasing using \(f'(x) = \frac{1 - x}{2\sqrt x(x+1)^2} \le 0\) for \(x \ge 1\).
Concludes convergence by the alternating series test.
questions.why: Both the numerator and the denominator grow, so decrease is not obvious from inspection; the derivative settles it. (The series does not converge absolutely, since \(b_n\) behaves like \(\frac1{\sqrt n}\).)

questions.prompt: For \(S = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^4}\), find the smallest \(n\) for which the alternating series estimation theorem guarantees \(|S - s_n| < 10^{-4}\).

sections.title: Alternating series and their error bound

sections.md:
The alternating series test covers only strictly alternating signs. For a series whose signs follow no pattern, such as \(\sum \frac{\sin n}{n^2}\), the practical approach is to discard the signs and apply the tests for nonnegative series to \(\sum |a_n|\). This section shows why that works, and why a series can behave differently from the series of its absolute values.

> **Definitions.** A series \(\sum a_n\) **converges absolutely** if \(\sum |a_n|\) converges. It **converges conditionally** if \(\sum a_n\) converges but \(\sum |a_n|\) diverges.

> **Theorem.** If \(\sum |a_n|\) converges, then \(\sum a_n\) converges.

*Proof.* For every \(n\), \(-|a_n| \le a_n \le |a_n|\), hence \(0 \le a_n + |a_n| \le 2|a_n|\). Since \(\sum 2|a_n|\) converges, the direct comparison test shows that \(\sum (a_n + |a_n|)\) converges. Then \(\sum a_n = \sum (a_n + |a_n|) - \sum |a_n|\) is a difference of convergent series, so it converges.

**Examples.** The signs of \(\frac{\sin n}{n^2}\) follow no regular pattern, but \(\left|\frac{\sin n}{n^2}\right| \le \frac{1}{n^2}\), so \(\sum \frac{\sin n}{n^2}\) converges absolutely and therefore converges. The series \(\sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}\) converges absolutely. The alternating harmonic series converges conditionally: it converges by the alternating series test, but its series of absolute values is the harmonic series.

**Classifying a series.** Every series is exactly one of absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent. To decide which:
1. Test \(\sum |a_n|\) with the tests for nonnegative series. If it converges, \(\sum a_n\) converges absolutely.
2. Otherwise, test \(\sum a_n\) itself, usually with the alternating series test or the divergence test. If it converges, it converges conditionally; if not, it diverges.

**Worked example.** Classify \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n n}{n^2 + 1}\). *Absolute values:* comparing \(\frac{n}{n^2+1}\) with \(\frac1n\) gives the ratio \(\frac{n^2}{n^2 + 1} \to 1\), so \(\sum \frac{n}{n^2 + 1}\) diverges by limit comparison with the harmonic series, and the series does not converge absolutely. *The series itself:* \(b_n = \frac{n}{n^2+1} \to 0\), and for \(f(x) = \frac{x}{x^2+1}\), \(f'(x) = \frac{1 - x^2}{(x^2+1)^2} \le 0\) when \(x \ge 1\), so \(\{b_n\}\) is nonincreasing. By the alternating series test the series converges. It therefore converges conditionally.

**Why the distinction matters.** A finite sum can be added in any order. An absolutely convergent series keeps this property: every rearrangement of its terms converges to the same sum. A conditionally convergent series does not. The **Riemann rearrangement theorem** states that the terms of a conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to converge to any prescribed real number, or to diverge. For instance, take the terms of the alternating harmonic series in the order one positive, two negative:
\[ \left(1 - \frac12 - \frac14\right) + \left(\frac13 - \frac16 - \frac18\right) + \left(\frac15 - \frac1{10} - \frac1{12}\right) + \cdots \]
The \(k\)th group is \(\frac{1}{2k-1} - \frac{1}{4k-2} - \frac{1}{4k} = \frac12\left(\frac{1}{2k-1} - \frac{1}{2k}\right)\), so the partial sums at the ends of the groups are half the partial sums \(s_{2k}\) of the alternating harmonic series. Since the terms tend to 0, the rearranged series converges to \(\frac12 \ln 2\), half the original sum. Conditional convergence depends on the order in which positive and negative terms cancel; absolute convergence does not depend on cancellation at all.

**Common mistakes.** Treating "alternating" and "conditionally convergent" as synonyms: \(\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\) alternates and converges absolutely. And concluding that \(\sum a_n\) diverges because \(\sum |a_n|\) diverges: that only rules out absolute convergence.

questions.model: *Absolute values.* For \(n \ge 2\), \(0 < \ln n < n\), so \(\frac1{\ln n} > \frac1n > 0\). The harmonic series (from \(n = 2\)) diverges, so \(\sum \frac1{\ln n}\) diverges by direct comparison, and the series is not absolutely convergent. *The series itself.* It alternates with \(b_n = \frac1{\ln n} > 0\). Since \(\ln\) is increasing, \(b_{n+1} < b_n\), and since \(\ln n \to \infty\), \(b_n \to 0\). By the alternating series test the series converges. Therefore it converges conditionally.
questions.prompt: Classify \(\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{\ln n}\) as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent. Justify both parts of the classification.
rubric: Shows \(\sum \frac{1}{\ln n}\) diverges, e.g. \(0 < \ln n < n\) gives \(\frac1{\ln n} > \frac1n\) and direct comparison with the harmonic series.
Verifies \(b_n = \frac1{\ln n}\) is positive, decreasing (since \(\ln\) is increasing) and tends to 0.
Concludes convergence by the alternating series test.
States the classification: conditionally convergent.
questions.why: The two-step procedure: first absolute values with a positive-term test, then the alternating series test on the original series.

questions.prompt: For which values of \(p\) does \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^p}\) converge conditionally?
questions.why: The series of absolute values is the \(p\)-series, convergent exactly for \(p > 1\); those \(p\) give absolute convergence, not conditional. For \(0 < p \le 1\), \(\frac{1}{n^p}\) decreases to 0, so the alternating series test gives convergence while \(\sum \frac1{n^p}\) diverges: conditional convergence. For \(p \le 0\) the terms do not tend to 0 and the series diverges. The option \"all \(p > 0\)\" confuses convergence with conditional convergence.

sections.md:
The comparison tests need a known series to compare with. For series built from factorials and exponentials, such as \(\sum \frac{n^2}{2^n}\) or \(\sum \frac{n!}{10^n}\), the right comparison is with a geometric series, made by measuring how fast the terms shrink. The ratio and root tests carry out that comparison automatically.

> **Ratio test.** Let \(\sum a_n\) have nonzero terms, and suppose \(L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|\) exists or is \(\infty\).
> 1. If \(L < 1\), the series converges absolutely.
> 2. If \(L > 1\) or \(L = \infty\), the series diverges.
> 3. If \(L = 1\), the test is inconclusive.

**Why it is true.** If \(L < 1\), choose \(r\) with \(L < r < 1\). For all \(n\) beyond some \(N\), \(|a_{n+1}| \le r|a_n|\), hence \(|a_{N+k}| \le |a_N|\, r^k\). The tail of \(\sum |a_n|\) is dominated by a convergent geometric series, so \(\sum a_n\) converges absolutely. If \(L > 1\), then eventually \(|a_{n+1}| > |a_n|\), so the terms do not tend to 0 and the divergence test applies. If \(L = 1\), both behaviours occur: for \(\sum \frac1n\) and \(\sum \frac{1}{n^2}\) the ratios \(\frac{n}{n+1}\) and \(\frac{n^2}{(n+1)^2}\) both tend to 1, yet the first series diverges and the second converges.

**Worked examples.** (1) \(\sum \frac{n^2}{2^n}\): \(\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \frac{(n+1)^2}{2^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{2^n}{n^2} = \frac12\left(1 + \frac1n\right)^2 \to \frac12 < 1\), so the series converges absolutely. (2) \(\sum \frac{n!}{10^n}\): the ratio is \(\frac{(n+1)!}{10^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{10^n}{n!} = \frac{n+1}{10} \to \infty\), so the series diverges. (3) \(\sum \frac{n^n}{n!}\): the ratio is \(\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\cdot\frac{n!}{n^n} = \left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n \to e > 1\), so the series diverges. In each case, simplify \(\frac{(n+1)!}{n!} = n+1\) before taking the limit.

> **Root test.** Suppose \(L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\) exists or is \(\infty\). If \(L < 1\), the series converges absolutely; if \(L > 1\) or \(L = \infty\), it diverges; if \(L = 1\), the test is inconclusive.

The reason is the same comparison: if \(L < r < 1\), then \(|a_n| \le r^n\) for all large \(n\). The root test suits terms that are \(n\)th powers. **Worked example.** For \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{2n+1}{3n-1}\right)^n\), \(\sqrt[n]{|a_n|} = \frac{2n+1}{3n-1} \to \frac23 < 1\), so the series converges absolutely.

**Choosing a test.** A workable order of questions:
1. Do the terms tend to 0? If not, the divergence test settles the matter.
2. Is it a geometric, \(p\)-, or telescoping series? Then the known results apply.
3. Do the terms contain factorials or powers \(c^n\)? Try the ratio test; if the whole term is an \(n\)th power, the root test.
4. Is the term a rational or algebraic expression in \(n\)? Use limit comparison with a \(p\)-series, taking \(b_n\) from the dominant parts.
5. Do the signs change? Test \(\sum |a_n|\) first; if that series diverges and the signs alternate, use the alternating series test.
6. Is \(a_n = f(n)\) for a decreasing \(f\) that you can integrate, such as \(\frac{1}{n(\ln n)^2}\)? Use the integral test.

**Common mistakes.** Applying the ratio test to rational expressions in \(n\): the limit is always 1, and nothing is learned. Checking that each ratio \(\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|\) is less than 1 instead of computing the limit: for the harmonic series every ratio \(\frac{n}{n+1}\) is less than 1, yet the series diverges. The test needs the limit to be less than 1, which keeps the ratios eventually below a fixed \(r < 1\). Finally, dropping the absolute value, which for alternating series produces a negative number that means nothing.

questions.prompt: For \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n!}{n^n}\), compute \(L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|\). Give the exact value.
questions.why: \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{(n+1)!}{(n+1)^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{n^n}{n!} = \frac{(n+1)\,n^n}{(n+1)^{n+1}} = \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n = \frac{1}{(1 + 1/n)^n} \to \frac1e\). Since \(\frac1e < 1\), the series converges absolutely.

questions.model: The terms are positive. \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{(2n+2)!}{(2n)!}\cdot\frac{(n!)^2}{((n+1)!)^2}\cdot\frac{5^n}{5^{n+1}} = \frac{(2n+2)(2n+1)}{(n+1)^2}\cdot\frac15 = \frac{2(2n+1)}{5(n+1)}\). As \(n\to\infty\) this tends to \(\frac{4}{5} < 1\). By the ratio test the series converges (absolutely).
questions.prompt: Determine whether \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(2n)!}{(n!)^2\,5^n}\) converges. Show the simplification of the ratio of consecutive terms.
rubric: Simplifies to \(\frac{(2n+2)(2n+1)}{5(n+1)^2}\).
Computes the limit \(\frac45 < 1\).
Concludes absolute convergence (hence convergence) by the ratio test.
questions.why: \(\frac{(2n+2)!}{(2n)!} = (2n+2)(2n+1)\): two factors, not one, because the argument of the factorial increases by 2.

questions.model: \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{n+2}{n+1}\cdot\frac{n^3 + 2}{(n+1)^3 + 2}\), and both factors tend to 1, so \(L = 1\) and the ratio test gives no information. This always happens for rational expressions in \(n\), which change by a factor close to 1 from one term to the next. Instead, the dominant parts give \(\frac{n}{n^3} = \frac1{n^2}\). With \(b_n = \frac1{n^2}\), \(\frac{a_n}{b_n} = \frac{n^3 + n^2}{n^3 + 2} \to 1\), positive and finite, and \(\sum \frac1{n^2}\) converges, so the series converges by the limit comparison test.
questions.prompt: Explain why the ratio test cannot decide the convergence of \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{n+1}{n^3 + 2}\), and then settle its convergence with an appropriate test.
rubric: Computes (or argues) that the ratio of consecutive terms of a rational expression tends to 1, so the ratio test is inconclusive.
Chooses limit comparison with \(\frac1{n^2}\) (dominant parts \(\frac{n}{n^3}\)).
Computes \(\lim \frac{n^3 + n^2}{n^3 + 2} = 1\).
Concludes convergence since \(\sum\frac1{n^2}\) is a \(p\)-series with \(p = 2 > 1\).
questions.why: Ratio and root tests detect geometric-type decay. Polynomial-type decay like \(\frac1{n^2}\) is invisible to them and belongs to comparison with \(p\)-series.

terms.d: An expression \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots\) formed from a sequence of terms; its value, if any, is the limit of its partial sums.
The finite sum \(s_n = a_1 + \cdots + a_n\) of the first \(n\) terms of a series.
The real number \(S = \lim_{n\to\infty} s_n\), when this limit exists; the series is then said to converge.
A series whose sequence of partial sums converges to a real number; otherwise the series is divergent.
A series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty ar^{n-1}\) with \(a \ne 0\); it converges to \(\frac{a}{1-r}\) if \(|r| < 1\) and diverges if \(|r| \ge 1\).
The constant \(r\) by which each term of a geometric series is multiplied to give the next term.
A series whose terms are differences \(b_n - b_{n+1}\), so that its partial sums collapse to \(b_1 - b_{n+1}\).
The series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1n\); it diverges although its terms tend to 0.
If \(\lim a_n\) does not exist or is not 0, then \(\sum a_n\) diverges; also called the \(n\)th-term test. It never proves convergence.
A series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^p}\); it converges if and only if \(p > 1\).
If \(f\) is continuous, positive and decreasing on \([1,\infty)\) and \(a_n = f(n)\), then \(\sum a_n\) and \(\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx\) both converge or both diverge.
The error \(R_n = S - s_n = \sum_{k=n+1}^\infty a_k\) made in approximating the sum of a convergent series by its \(n\)th partial sum.
If \(0 \le a_n \le b_n\) eventually, convergence of \(\sum b_n\) implies convergence of \(\sum a_n\), and divergence of \(\sum a_n\) implies divergence of \(\sum b_n\).
If \(a_n, b_n > 0\) and \(\frac{a_n}{b_n} \to c\) with \(0 < c < \infty\), then \(\sum a_n\) and \(\sum b_n\) both converge or both diverge.
A series of the form \(\sum (-1)^{n+1} b_n\) or \(\sum(-1)^n b_n\) with every \(b_n > 0\).
If \(b_n > 0\), \(\{b_n\}\) is (eventually) nonincreasing and \(b_n \to 0\), then \(\sum(-1)^{n+1}b_n\) converges, and \(|R_n| \le b_{n+1}\).
\(\sum a_n\) converges absolutely if \(\sum|a_n|\) converges; absolute convergence implies convergence.
\(\sum a_n\) converges conditionally if it converges but \(\sum |a_n|\) diverges.

A series containing exactly the same terms as \(\sum a_n\) in a different order. Absolutely convergent series keep their sum under rearrangement; conditionally convergent ones can be rearranged to any sum (Riemann rearrangement theorem).
With \(L = \lim\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|\): \(L < 1\) gives absolute convergence, \(L > 1\) (or \(\infty\)) divergence, \(L = 1\) no conclusion.
With \(L = \lim\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\): \(L < 1\) gives absolute convergence, \(L > 1\) (or \(\infty\)) divergence, \(L = 1\) no conclusion.
